claims.text: Laser-heated aerodynamic levitation with fast in situ calorimetry and pyrometry enables accurate determination of melting temperature in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed setup enables accurate determination of fusion enthalpy in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed setup enables accurate determination of fusion entropy in high-entropy alloys.
The proposed setup enables accurate determination of volume change at melting in high-entropy alloys.
Non-contact aerodynamic levitation eliminates or substantially reduces container effects.
Rapid measurement captures the thermal transitions associated with melting.
Rapid laser heating can operate at heating rates on the order of 10^3–10^4 K/s in the proposed setup.
Melting during levitation produces a freely suspended liquid droplet.
A freely suspended liquid droplet minimizes container-induced heterogeneities.
Aerodynamic levitation prevents contact-induced nucleation.
Aerodynamic levitation prevents contact-induced contamination.
The proposed method can measure melting temperatures with an accuracy of ±10 K.
The proposed method can determine fusion enthalpy with errors below 5–10%.
The proposed method can determine fusion entropy with errors below 5–10%.
The proposed method can determine volume change at melting with precision comparable to 5–10%.
The stated quantitative performance applies across the high-entropy-alloy family.
Traditional container-based calorimetry is more prone to contamination than the proposed non-contact method.
Traditional container-based calorimetry and slower heating methods are more prone to calibration problems than the proposed method.
The approach may not translate directly to systems requiring slower kinetics or lower-temperature measurements.
Extreme heating rates can reduce the accuracy of fast pyrometric and calorimetric measurements unless advanced calibration is used.

contradictions.description: The conditions allow operation under vacuum, but aerodynamic levitation requires a gas flow or surrounding fluid to provide aerodynamic support. Vacuum operation is therefore incompatible with the stated levitation mechanism unless a separate levitation method or a nonzero-pressure gas environment is specified.
